subject: machine-learning
question: Does fast training mean k-NN will also be fast at prediction time?

artifact.plan:
Serve a k-NN classifier (k = 5) over 20 million stored examples, answering each API request in under 20 ms.
AI note: "k-NN trains instantly, so it will be fast in production too."

ai_claim: Yes. k-NN needs no training at all, so it is a fast model and predictions will easily meet 20 ms.

ai_solution.text: k-NN does no work at training time.
It simply stores the data.
A model that trains instantly is fast.
So predictions will be fast.

failure.misconception: Confusing cheap training with cheap prediction
failure.explanation: k-NN defers all work to prediction: each query must find the nearest of 20 million stored points. A brute-force search computes 20 million distances per request, far beyond 20 ms. k-NN is a 'lazy' learner. Use an approximate nearest-neighbour index, reduce the data, or choose a model whose prediction cost is independent of training size.

canonical_solution: No: prediction scans (or indexes) all 20 million examples per query. Use an ANN index or a different model.

valid_evidence.summary: 20,000,000 distances x 50 dimensions = 10^9 operations per request.
k-NN's prediction cost grows with the training set size.

counterexamples: Each request compares the query with every stored example.

hints.text: Ask where k-NN does its work.
Step 3 generalises from training speed.
k-NN is lazy: all computation happens at query time.
Count the distances per request.
Step 3 is wrong: prediction is expensive with 20 million points.

repair: Use an approximate nearest-neighbour index (e.g. HNSW) or a parametric model.
debrief: Account for both training and inference costs. Lazy learners shift cost to inference, where latency limits live.

subject: machine-learning
question: Is the reviewer right that duplicated words leave the predictions unchanged?

artifact.change: A spam filter (multinomial Naive Bayes on word counts) gets a new feature pipeline that accidentally includes every word twice (the title is copied into the body).
artifact.claim_in_review: "Duplicating features does not change Naive Bayes predictions; it just repeats the same evidence."

ai_claim: Yes. The duplicate words carry the same information, so the classifier's predictions stay the same.

ai_solution.text: Every word now appears twice.
Duplicates add no new information.
So the posterior probabilities stay the same.
Predictions are unchanged.

failure.misconception: Forgetting that Naive Bayes treats features as independent evidence
failure.explanation: Naive Bayes multiplies the likelihood of each feature as if they were independent. Duplicating every word squares each likelihood ratio, doubling the log-odds contribution of the text. Probabilities become far more extreme (overconfident), and borderline messages can flip class when the prior is fixed. The independence assumption is exactly what duplicates violate.

canonical_solution: No: duplicated features are counted as independent evidence, squaring likelihood ratios and making predictions overconfident (and sometimes different).

valid_evidence.summary: A word with likelihood ratio 3 contributes ln 3 = 1.10 to the log-odds once, 2.20 when duplicated.
A message at log-odds -0.5 from its words plus a prior of +0.8 is spam (0.3); duplicated, -1.0 + 0.8 = -0.2 flips it to ham.

counterexamples: Borderline messages change class after duplication.

hints.text: Recall how Naive Bayes combines features.
Step 3 assumes the model knows the features are duplicates.
The model multiplies likelihoods as if features were independent.
Compute log-odds with and without duplication.
Step 3 is wrong: duplicates are double-counted, changing and sharpening predictions.

repair: Remove duplicated text; watch for correlated features in Naive Bayes.
debrief: The 'naive' assumption means correlated features are over-counted. Naive Bayes often ranks well but produces poorly calibrated probabilities for this reason.

subject: machine-learning
question: For a spam email containing 'invoice' along with 20 strongly spammy words, can this classifier still rate it as spam?

artifact.code:
# Hand-written Naive Bayes, no smoothing:
# P(word | spam) = count(word in spam) / total spam words
# The word 'invoice' never appeared in the spam training emails.
score_spam = prior_spam * prod(P(w | spam) for w in email_words)

ai_claim: Yes. One unseen word has little effect; the 20 spammy words dominate, so the email is still rated spam.

ai_solution.text: The email contains 20 strongly spammy words.
'invoice' is only one word.
One word has little influence on the product.
So the email is rated spam.

failure.misconception: Letting an unseen word zero the whole product
failure.explanation: P('invoice' | spam) = 0 / N = 0, and multiplying by 0 makes score_spam exactly 0, whatever the other 20 words say. The email can never be classified as spam. Laplace (add-one) smoothing - (count + 1) / (N + V) - gives unseen words a small non-zero probability.
failure.why_convincing: Intuitively, one word among twenty should matter little.

canonical_solution: No: the zero probability for 'invoice' makes the spam score 0. Use Laplace smoothing.

valid_evidence.summary: With add-one smoothing, P('invoice' | spam) = 1 / (N + V) > 0, and the email is rated spam.

counterexamples: Any email with a word unseen in spam training is always ham.

hints.text: Compute P('invoice' | spam).
Step 3 assumes one factor cannot dominate a product.
A single zero factor makes a product zero.
Multiply the likelihoods including the zero.
Step 3 is wrong: the zero makes the spam score 0. Use Laplace smoothing.

repair: Use Laplace smoothing: P(w | c) = (count + 1) / (N_c + V).
debrief: Products of probabilities are fragile: one zero dominates everything. Smoothing and log-space sums are standard defences.

subject: machine-learning
question: Will the linear SVM classify all four training points correctly?

artifact.plan: LinearSVC(C=1000) - "a large C forces the SVM to classify every training point correctly."

ai_claim: Yes. A very large C penalises misclassification heavily, so the SVM will find a line that separates the classes perfectly.

ai_solution.text: C controls the penalty for misclassified points.
With C = 1000, errors are very costly.
So the SVM finds a boundary with no errors.
All four points are classified correctly.

failure.misconception: Expecting a penalty to create separability
failure.explanation: This is the XOR pattern: no straight line separates {(0,0), (1,1)} from {(0,1), (1,0)}. A large C only makes the optimiser try harder; the best any linear boundary can do is 3 of 4 correct. A non-linear kernel (e.g. RBF or polynomial) or a feature such as x1 x x2 is needed.
failure.why_convincing: Large C does drive training error to zero - when the data are linearly separable.

canonical_solution: No: XOR is not linearly separable, so at most 3 of the 4 points can be correct. Use a non-linear kernel or add x1 x x2.

valid_evidence.summary: Any line that puts (0,0) and (1,1) on one side must also put (0,1) or (1,0) there.
With the feature x1 x x2 added, a linear boundary separates the classes.

counterexamples: No line separates the XOR classes.

hints.text: Try drawing a line that separates the two classes.
Step 3 assumes a perfect linear boundary exists.
C cannot create separability that the feature space lacks.
Plot the four points.
Step 3 is wrong: XOR is not linearly separable. Use a non-linear kernel.

repair: Use an RBF or polynomial kernel, or add the interaction feature x1 x x2.
debrief: Model capacity is set by the hypothesis class, not by regularisation settings. A linear model cannot represent XOR, whatever C is.

subject: machine-learning
question: Is the AI's reading of the table correct?
ai_claim: Yes. Larger C penalises margin violations more, so the SVM fits the training data more tightly with fewer support vectors and a narrower margin. Training accuracy rises, but validation accuracy peaks at C = 1 and drops at C = 100: overfitting.

ai_solution.text: C sets the cost of margin violations.
Larger C gives a narrower margin and fewer support vectors (1,420 -> 310).
Training accuracy rises to 0.99.
Validation accuracy is best at C = 1 (0.87), so C = 100 overfits.

canonical_solution: Correct. C trades margin width against training errors; validation performance chooses C = 1 here.

hints.text: Relate C to the margin.
Step 2 connects C to the number of support vectors.
Large C means a hard margin that fits training data closely.
Find the best validation accuracy.
This solution is correct. C = 1 balances fit and generalisation. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: C is a regularisation knob with the opposite convention to lambda: larger C, less regularisation. Validation curves choose it.
